questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: One thing was the academic institution and opportunities, which I did factor into my decision, but I would say that the biggest reason of them all was that I wanted to experience a new place and culture. I also thought that if I would go on exchange I would want to go far away and to a place I've never been and would want to visit.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was really happy that I chose to go, and I had an amazing time, the reason i didn't give a 10/10 was because the process to get to go and registering and everything was pretty stressful and tedious.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I think I managed pretty well. Course registration was a bit hard to figure out, but doing the test round helped a lot for me. You'll need a lot of documents and when you arrive you should apply for an ARC, but the korean sites are pretty hard to navigate. I know some exchange students did their ARC application and so on through HireVisa, so they did group applications. But I found that I got my ARC before the group one.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was an orientiation but not everyone could attend because of limited space. But mostly you will also figure out a lot of the stuff from other exchange students. The most confusing part for me was how attendance worked, since it differed from class to class

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: They did help out, but a lot of it you still need to figure out yourself how it works even though they give you the apps that help a lot. I signed up with the Buddy program and I was really happy I did that and if I were to go again I would 100% apply for it again. There you can also ask some of the local students how stuff works if you are unsure.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: You could also say I found it through my host insitution, but i just did it through an agency called Ziptoss which was also listed on the Universities website. Ziptoss connected me to a landlord and landlady and I managed to rent out a one-room studio, but not a goshiwon. I had a great experience with my housing, but I don't know if I would call the process easy since I signed and payed deposit before even arriving in Korea, so I felt pretty scared of getting scammed. But I didn't and that is just how it's done there. There are dorms but it wasn't worth the work for me since it is lottery based. I lived by SNU station and from there you can easily take the shuttlebus to campus for free, and it takes max. 10 min. I paid around 900.000 krw pr. month which is more than some other students payed but I had my own space that was a little bigger with really nice facilities, and god floor heating.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It's not too hard to find places to live off campus that are close to campus with nice access, some good areas are Gwanak-gu and arounf SNU station, and Sillim and in the Venture Town. There are tons of goshiwons which are pretty small but cheap, but most exchange students lived there, also since you won't be at home a lot of the time anyway. Though i went for a one-room studio which can be a bit more expensive but for me it was worth it. I was also allowed to have friends over, which you typically are not allowed in goshiwons.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It went really well for me and for a lot of other people. I only know of few people that had a bit of and off-puuting experience, but really not that many.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Super tedious, and it was hard to understand where in the process you were. Google was my best friend. In terms of course registration it's on first come first served basis and it was a bit hard to understand at first.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Well all classes for the semester isn't released until july, then you can but them in a wishlist or liked, so you can see how popular the course is. You will also be able to see how many spots there are in the course. Then first they have a pre-registration period, which is just a trail registration so nothing you register for during this period counts. Like a trail run. Then later comes the real period. Apply for the most popular courses first! and look out for restrictions. Then later comes the add and drop period, where you can drop courses you have and add new ones. in this period it might be possible for you to add a popular course you maybe couldn't get because the quota was met. So if someone drops it you can add it if you are fast. If you still don't get a course you want because of quota or anything else, you can email the professor to ask them to add you and send an exceeding quato registration request, when that opens.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: some guides on their webpage and they sent out emails with information about it.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got almost all the courses I wanted except for one, because of restrictions, but I didn't end up having many courses related to my major since I lot of them were either not within my prerequisites or courses I had already completed at home.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Just try to get the hang of the system a bit before and you will be fine, no need to panic too much. I used the course list from the years before to get an idea of which courses might be there for the semester i went.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It's was a bit strange to me. One was way too hard espcially for bachelor students that haven't done differetial equations, while the others seemed more like high school level courses, and mostly relied on memorization. I think it also depends a lot on the course and department.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: As mentioned in my comment it was weird. They also do not do exercise classes and basically all of it is just powerpoints or notes from the teacher every week. I did not use or have to acquire a single book.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I think I like the style of teaching more at UCPH since I find it more structured. Overall it was just a weird experience with course levels at SNU.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Topics in Mathematics 2, Extraterrestrial Planets and Life, Korean History and 13 week Korean Language Program at LEI.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I found Extraterrestrial Planets and Life to be a really fun and interesting course. Not a super high level so It's pretty nice and easy to follow, even if it has nothing to do with your major. It was also interesting to take Korean History especially while living in Korea, and the language program for me I found fun and also helpful to take while being in Korea.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
It wasn't really unexpected since I knew about it already but it cost more than I thought and the process to apply to not pay it was a lot of work. But once your get your ARC and are registered you will start recieving NHIS bills, which is sthe National Health Insurance in Korea, but I already had payed and insurance from back home, i used Europæiske Erv, which was around 1800 dkk for 5-6 months. So my insurance bill is pretty high since I basically payed for doubble insurance.

Also you have to pay around 30.000 krw for your ARC application, and every month i payed very little for electricity.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Eating out is suuuper cheap, and also you can get lunch on campus (and dinner) for as little as 4.5 dkk at one of the cafeterias. Fruit and vegetable are expensive and it basically makes no sense to cook at home. 

I wanna point out that I tried to overestimate a lot of the costs above.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: They have a lot of clubs but I didn't see a reason to join any since I probably wouldn't have much time to go since I was only there for one semester. I have no idea how easy they are to join.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I went hiking and played basket like two times with my buddy group, one of the basket practices I more or less organized though, but hiking is also really fun! Also tons of board game cafes and I went to karaoke a lot. But most of it was done privatly and not through the host insitution. With the Buddy program there is a thurday pub every thurday where you can go hang out. One thing is also the SNU festival were there was music and food stalls it was worth it in my opinion to go. It's free entry and all you do is show your student card. Also it's fun to check out the club fair when they are there.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The SNU festival as I said before, and The Buddy program was the best decision. Also maybe I should add that you do need to pay a bit to enter the program. They do a lot of social activities so usually you'll be able to go to stuff through that, and alsio meet people!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I went to Busan and it was super nice. I didn't manage to but I also really wanted to go see Danyang, I'll totally plan a trip to go there if I ever visit again. After the semester ended in December I went to Japan, and it was also really cool. I would also recommend to go Hiking, if you are there during autumn you should go when all the leaves turn red and yellow, it's crazy beautiful! It's like Korea was made for Autumn to exist. Also check out some of the fancy and special cafes.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Not too hard, it was not that different from back home in regards to how people interact, and almost all koreans I spoke with were so nice! Queue culture is a bit weird sometimes they are great at it and other times really bad. But it's pretty easy to adjust to. First you need to get used to people (mostly elderly) staring.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join the Buddy Program. Local students don't really often speak to you and it can be hard to break the ice.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: People walk really really slow... It was just really annoying, but nothing was particularly really challenging in my opinion.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: how friendly people are and how convenient everything is.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: I would take part in the Buddy Program, research how some of the processes in terms of registering yourself and everything works beforehand just to give yourself a sense of calmness maybe take passport photos in Denmark, since they like to use filters a lot in Korea. Lastly maybe try some of the things that you don't see in Denmark, and try going to see a lot of the different areas also other university Campuses, and just keep a lookout on you KUmail a lot up until you start university there.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I think I've mentioned the most important things. I can't think of a lot more right now

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The people I got to meet, and trying to experience living abroad. I feel I grew a lot as a person having to navigate everything and do so many things on my own, and kind of trying to integrate a bit into another country and society.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Maybe when you miss home sometimes, also at the start before the semester started and I had met people, I had a hard time getting myself to eat, because the getting used to everything was so overwhelming. But the second you start being around people and everything it all became so much easier.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: not really

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
